content: Ramadan is the Islamic month of fasting — Muslims abstain from food, drink, and smoking from fajr (pre-dawn) to maghrib (sunset). In Indonesia (world's largest Muslim country) many warungs close during daylight or draw a curtain across the front; some fully close for the month. Business hours shift; expect reduced service. After sunset, buka puasa (breaking of the fast) begins — bazaars pop up nationwide selling takjil (sweet snacks) + iftar meals. Non-Muslims are welcome to eat at hotels and non-halal restaurants; being discreet in public during daylight is a courtesy. Runs a lunar month (varies annually).

Idul Fitri (Lebaran, Eid al-Fitr) marks the end of Ramadan — Indonesia's biggest annual holiday. The two official public holidays surround a national exodus (mudik) as millions travel to their family village. Transport prices spike 2–3× for the week either side; airports, trains, ferries fully booked. Jakarta becomes eerily quiet; tourist areas continue normally. Halal bi halal (mutual forgiveness visits) fill the days after. Book any long-distance travel 2 months ahead of Lebaran week.

Idul Adha (Eid al-Adha) is the Islamic 'Feast of Sacrifice', ~70 days after Idul Fitri. Sheep, goats, and cows are ritually sacrificed at mosques nationwide; meat is distributed to the poor. Public holiday. Less travel disruption than Idul Fitri but expect some restaurant menu changes (more mutton, goat curry). Non-Muslims visiting a mosque during the ceremony should ask permission and dress modestly.
